title: Search in a BST
statement:
You are given the root of a binary search tree (BST) and an integer `val`. Every node holds a distinct integer; for each node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger.

Find the node whose value equals `val` and report the **subtree rooted at that node**. If no node holds `val`, report that the value is absent.

The tree is given in level order with `null` for missing children (the children of a `null` entry are not listed). The subtree is printed in the same format: level order, with `null` for missing children, and without trailing `null` entries. If `val` does not occur in the tree, print `null`.
inputFormat:
The first line contains the tree in level order: space-separated tokens, each an integer or the word `null`. The first token is the root and is never `null`.
The second line contains the integer `val`.
outputFormat: Print the level-order serialization of the subtree rooted at the node with value `val`, space-separated, or the single word `null` if there is no such node.
constraints: The depth of the tree is at most 5000

examples.explanation: The node with value 2 is the left child of the root. Its subtree has 2 as its root with children 1 and 3.
Searching for 5: 5 > 4 so go right to 7, 5 < 7 so go left, but 7 has no left child. The value is not present.
Node 3 has no left child and has the right child 4, so its subtree is printed as 3 null 4.

tests.input:
30 21 31 14 null null 32 4 17 null null 2 6 null null null 3 null 10 null null 7 11
21
tests.output: 21 14 null 4 17 2 6 null null null 3 null 10 null null 7 11

complexity.time: O(h) for the search, where h is the tree height (parsing and printing are O(n))

hints: You are given a BST, so you never need to look at both children of a node.
Compare val with the current node: smaller means go left, larger means go right, equal means you are done.
This can be written as a simple loop, so it does not need recursion.
